speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: REPORT OF DELEGATE ON THIRTY-FIFTH COMMONWEALTH PARLIAMENTARY CONFERENCE
speechtext: Introduction of government bills.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I recognize the important issue that we are going to be discussing today on the motion of the Official Opposition.
Some time back I wrote a letter on behalf of my caucus to the Government House Leader indicating that if there was a need to introduce legislation to continue the variable entrance rates for the Unemployment Insurance Act, we would be prepared to do that expeditiously, and we would pass it with virtually no debate.
The point of my intervention is that I think we all appreciate the importance of the opposition day motion and I wonder if we could not save time and get on with other business by simply agreeing unanimously, if the need arises, to pass this legislation with no debate before the Christmas recess. It would allow us to get on with other business.
Just to ensure that my colleagues in the Official Opposition do not misinterpret what I am saying, I recognize this is their opposition day. We would be prepared to give up one of our opposition days to them on some other issue.
I wonder if we could perhaps seek unanimous consent to see if we could agree to introduce this necessary legislation without going through and spending a whole day debating its merits.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to make a few comments. First, one can hardly give up something one does not have. The two opposition days, today and tomorrow, happen to be days for the Official Opposition, not the third party in this House. I remind the government that it cannot start negotiating on the floor of the House something that it does not have.
Second, with respect to the overwhelming support of Bill C-21, I remind the minister that on both occasions they had to invoke closure to get the bill through the House. That is hardly what I call overwhelming support. It was a Tory promotion, a Tory-supported bill. It was not supported by the opposition nor by the Official Opposition. The minister's memory is getting shorter as he gets a little older. Indeed, closure on these matters is repugnant to Canadians and we will make that message clear in today's debate.
The point of today's debate is to get this government to understand that there are Canadians who will suffer because of this government's lack of tiying to answer a very serious situation in this country where those who may be on the unemployment insurance program will not get the benefits of that program next year because of this government's failure to come to grips with legislation that is required urgently.

I regret that my hon. colleague did not see fit to accept my recommendation but perhaps that will be possible on another day. I want to echo the words of the opposition Whip that Bill C-21 is not a bill that this House unanimously adopted by any stretch of the imagination. Any piece of legislation that would adversely affect over one million Canadians financially is something that we, on this side of the House, certainly want nothing to do with. In an effort to co-operate and to get on with some good legislation eventually, we thought we would make this offer today. I appreciate that the government House leader will at least give it some thought in the future.

speechtext:

Madam Speaker, the people here join the many thousands of other Canadians in protesting strongly this government's intention to impose a hidden 9 per cent sales tax on goods and services starting in January, 1991. The Canadians who signed this petition maintain that to have hidden taxes applying virtually to everything is a



new imposition on Canadians. They strongly oppose this tax as an unprecedented tax grab from the pockets of Canadians that not only will result in higher taxes for those who can least afford it, that is those on low and middle incomes, but will produce higher inflation, higher interest rates and higher unemployment in this country, things we hardly need today.

Madam Speaker, I believe Your Honour is about to call Orders of the Day.
I want to raise a point of order because I think we in the opposition have a legitimate objection to voice today concerning the procedure that has been adopted by the government.
On Wednesday last when we were sitting, the government announced the order of business for today as being, as I recall it, the continuation of report stage and third reading of Bill C-19 followed by report stage and third
December 5, 1989

reading of Bill C-15, the plant breeders' rights legislation.
Yesterday at five o'clock, the Minister of Justice came into the House. In fact it was shortly after five o'clock. He designated today as an opposition day. I recognize, as do all hon. members, that the government has the right to decide the order of business, but if we are to conduct the business of this House in anything like an orderly way I fail to understand why the government would even presume to make a change of this magnitude in the order of business to force an opposition day by surprise on us at five o'clock the previous day.
Members know that we have to give notice of our motion, and we managed to do that by six o'clock as required by the rules, but I submit that this is a totally unprecedented and improper way to deal with the business of this House.
If the government expects co-operation from the opposition in orderly debate as they have been getting-bills have been sailing through this place it seems to me-I do not understand why it would take this step. I recognize the right is there but I want to express, on behalf of the opposition, our complete abhorrence of this procedure that has been followed.
Had I known last night when the minister stood up and made the announcement that there had been no discussions about that possibility in advance of it, I would have been on my feet and objected. I was in the House at the time but I had no idea-I only assumed that there had been negotiations. I understand there have been none. That was a completely irresponsible act on the part of the government that, in my view, was uncalled for. I know the minister would apologize if he were here. I hope he will have his parliamentary assistant apologize for really an unprecedented and improper use of the rules of this House.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT
ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should give urgent consideration to introducing in the immediate future a bill to extend the variable re-entry provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act in order to assure full protection of workers in economically distressed regions;
That this House declare its willingness to pass such a measure in no more than one sitting; and
That, for greater certainty, this House declare that the passage of this motion does not constitute a vote of no-confidence in the government.

December 5, 1989
Supply
He said: Madam Speaker, let me explain the purpose of this rather complicated motion. I want to say immediately that there is a slight typographical error in the motion. In the fourth line where it says "extend the variable re-entry provisions", that should read "the variable entry provisions". But the principle of the motion is the same and I think most members understand that we mean variable entry provisions.
According to Section 6 of the Unemployment Insurance Act of 1971, individuals need 14 weeks to qualify for unemployment insurance benefits. They need 14 weeks to qualify unless, of course, they are new entries into the workforce and then they need 20 weeks to qualify.
However, in 1977, the government of the day, a Liberal government at that time, introduced what is known as the variable entrance requirement whereby individuals would only need from 10 to 14 weeks to qualify for unemployment insurance benefits, depending on the rate of unemployment in their region. If they were living in a region which had very high unemployment, then they would only need 10 weeks to qualify for benefits. If they were living in a region with rather low unemployment, they would need 14 weeks. If the rate of unemployment was somewhere in between they would need 11, 12, or 13 weeks to qualify.
That was known as the variable entrance requirement and that was introduced in 1977 in a short one-page bill, but it was only introduced for the following year, 1978. It terminated at the end of the year.
From that year on, every year the government of the day re-introduced the variable entrance requirement for one year only, usually in the month of December, and it did it with a short one-paragraph or one-clause bill which extended this variable entrance requirement for the following year.
For one reason or another that I do not understand, neither the Liberal governments of Mr. Trudeau nor the Conservative governments of Mr. Clark or Mr. Mulro-ney made this a permanent thing. They simply extended it from year to year, always doing it in the month of December in a short one-page bill, and there was very little debate on that bill, usually lasting half a day.
The last time that this variable entrance requirement was extended was with Bill C-158, on September 29,
1988,	just before the call of the last election. Bill C-158 extended the variable entrance requirement for all of
1989,	this year, until January 6, 1990, when it expires. So the variable entrance requirement of 10 to 14 weeks will expire on January 6, 1990. That is where we stand with the variable entrance requirement.
This year, as all members know, the government introduced and passed in this House Bill C-21 which implemented very extensive changes to the unemployment insurance program. It introduced rather massive cuts to the benefits, made it more difficult to qualify, increased penalties for those who quit without just cause and terminated the government's contribution to the unemployment insurance fund, which last year was $2.8 billion.
In other words, Bill C-21 brought about very extensive changes in the unemployment insurance program, including a change whereby to qualify for unemployment insurance, one would require 10 to 20 weeks. That provision in Bill C-21 which sets out the qualifying period as ranging from 10 to 20 weeks would replace the 14-weeks' qualification period which is found in Section 6 of the Unemployment Insurance Act of 1971 and would also replace the 10 to 14 week variable entrance requirement which we have had year by year since 1977.
Bill C-21 was passed in this House on the evening of November 6. Bill C-21 went to the Senate on November 7, but as hon. members know, Parliament did not sit from November 11 to November 19 for the Remembrance Day recess and immediately after that, the Senate started debate on the bill and sent it to its committee last week. Committee hearings have already started in the Senate.
The problem is this. As I said, Bill C-21 introduces rather extensive changes to the unemployment insurance program. There is a reduction of benefits of $1.5 billion, which money is allocated to other purposes. There is an increased cost to employers and employees. There is a shift to welfare systems because if workers do not qualify for unemployment insurance or their benefits are terminated sooner and they do not have work, then
December 5, 1989

they have to rely on welfare, and welfare is taken care of by provinces and municipalities.
There is a loss to provinces due to the fact that moneys which went into provinces in the form of benefits will no longer go into those provinces to the same degree, and consequently the provinces do not know whether some of the developmental moneys will go to them to the same extent as the benefits did. In any case, Bill C-21 implements very extensive changes to the unemployment insurance system and I think the government would admit that itself. The government thinks those changes are good. We do not think they are very good.
Last year, there were 2.2 million claimants under the unemployment insurance program. That is a great number of Canadians. Some claims were for regular benefits and some were for the special benefits. The program last year was an $ 11-billion-plus program. The unemployment insurance program is the largest income-support program in Canada.
As I say, the bill went to the Senate on November 7. There was the recess for Remembrance Day of one week, and the Senate has started its hearings. I received information this morning that the Clerk of the Senate has already received 159 requests from groups and individuals asking to be heard on this bill, because they feel it impacts, in one way or another, on them and on the people they represent.
I also point out that in the House of Commons while we had committee hearings in the fall for four weeks and we heard as many groups as we could, we still turned down a large number of groups. We turned down, in fact, 127 individuals and groups, some for good reason but some simply because we did not have the time, due to the fact that we had to report the bill back by a fixed date.
The Senate is faced with a situation where it has had a very high number of requests to be heard on this bill by people who seriously want to give their views, and these people will have to be heard before December 22 when the Christmas recess starts. It is impossible for the Senate to dispose of Bill C-21 by that date. To have proper hearings, it would have to advertise and it would have to give groups time to prepare their briefs and so on. That is just the proper thing to do.
Supply
We are not talking about the Senate blocking the bill or unduly delaying the bill. We are talking about giving the Senate a reasonable amount of time to deal with those groups that want to be heard.
While we heard from a lot of trade unions, social groups, chambers of commerce and so on in the House of Commons committee, we did not hear from any provincial governments or provincial ministers, although some wanted to be heard. The Premier of New Brunswick wanted to be heard. Ministers from Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland and Nova Scotia wanted to be heard. We had to make a decision that we could not hear them.
We also did not hear from Mr. Forget who was the chairman of the royal commission established by the Conservative government in the last Parliament. He had spent more than a year studying the unemployment insurance program, but we did not hear from him. We did not hear from the Economic Council or from the Canadian Council for Labour Market Productivity or from other academics. We heard from a lot of grassroots groups, but we did not hear from a lot of people who wanted to be heard and should have been heard.
If Bill C-21 is not passed by January 6, and if the government does not bring in the usual bill to extend the variable entrance requirement, then it means that the standard flat qualification period across the country will be 14 weeks. If that is the case, that goes against the government's own policy of having a minimum qualification period of 10 weeks. It means that everybody will require 14 weeks to qualify until Bill C-21 is passed or unless the government introduces the variable entrance requirement.
The way to overcome this, and I say this in good faith and with the hope that the government will listen to reason, is to bring in once again either a one-page bill to extend the variable entrance requirement like the government did in September 1988 through Bill C-158, or put to the House a resolution which is provided for in Bill C-158 simply to extend the variable entrance requirement for two or three months. That is just enough time to give the Senate time to have a reasonable amount of time for hearings on Bill C-21.
According to my reading of Bill C-158, it allows the government to introduce a resolution which is approved by the Governor in Council to extend the variable entrance requirement for a time that could be open to negotiation, whether it was for two, three or four months or whatever. I suggest to the government that is another

Supply
way of doing this, either by a bill or by a resolution as provided for in Bill C-158.
We want to make clear that if the government did introduce such a bill to extend the variable entrance requirement, or if it introduced a resolution to extend it, we in this party would pass such a bill or resolution without any debate whatsoever. In the motion put to the House, we say we would pass it in less than one sitting. I give the commitment that we would not debate it at all. The motion or the resolution would be passed in a few minutes, as far as we are concerned.
We also say in this motion that we do not consider this motion to be a want of confidence motion. It is simply a plea to the government to do what it has done and what other governments have done year after year in the month of December, and that is to extend the variable entrance requirement.
7 I want to repeat that we are talking about the largest social income support program in Canada. It is a program that has ranged between $11 and $13 billion per year. This bill introduces massive changes to the program. The government thinks they are good changes, and we do not think they are. Some of them are good. Some of the provisions with respect to parental care and so on and benefits for senior citizens we approve of, but most of the bill we do not approve of, but that is beside the point. The point is that many Canadians are affected by this bill and they want to be heard. It is their democratic right to be heard.
I also point out to the government that it used closure at both second and third reading on this bill. At second reading, we only had one full day and two half days of debate. At third reading and report stage, we only had three and a half days of debate.
Another reason the government should consider introducing the variable entrance requirement or extending it for a period of time is that the government itself in Bill C-21 accepted that the minimum period for qualification should be 10 weeks, and I cannot understand why it would penalize people by allowing the 14-week minimum to apply for a month or two while Canadian groups are being heard on Bill C-21. If government members really believe that 10 weeks should be the minimum period for qualification in high unemployment regions,
then they should introduce the variable entrance requirement bill.
Another reason why they should do this is that the day after we completed the debate and the vote on third reading on Bill C-21 in this House, the government produced its new program for new unemployment insurance regions. This means that when we were discussing and debating Bill C-21, we did not know what those new regions would be.
When the groups that appeared before the House of Commons committee made their points known, they did not know what those new regions would be. As a matter of fact, those new regions changed the impact of Bill C-21. This is a further reason why we should allow the Senate a reasonable period of time to hear views on the bill now that those many groups know the proposals for the new regions.
In conclusion, let me sum up by saying that by this motion we are asking the government simply to extend the variable entrance requirement as it has done every year since it has taken office, as Liberal governments before it did, as the Clark government did. We ask the government to extend the variable entrance requirement by a bill or by a motion but not necessarily for a year as in the past, but simply for a fixed period of time which is a reasonable period of time to complete the hearings on Bill C-21 in the Senate. I am sure that that extension can be negotiated in a reasonable way in good faith.
We are asking that the government extend the variable entrance requirement because it is totally unreasonable to ask the Senate to finish its debate on Bill C-21 before Christmas. It is unreasonable to ask that because 159 groups have asked to be heard. I am not saying that all those groups deserve to be heard but at least half of them will be reasonable.
I have the list of groups wishing to be heard here. I could go through the list. They are from all parts of the country. Some of them are associations of adoptive parents, some of them are consumer counselling groups, some of them are trade unions, some of them are business associations and so on. I am not saying that all the groups that have asked the Senate to be heard should be heard, but certainly a good number of them should.
December 5, 1989

We are asking that because these people want to be heard on a major matter. This is not a minor matter. This is a very important bill. As I said, it deals with a program that last years was worth $11 billion. In the bill, the government cuts back benefits by $1.5 billion and relocates those moneys. Last year, there were 2.2 million claimants under the unemployment insurance program. That is a lot of Canadians and these people have a right to be heard.
With respect to the regions and the provinces, the impact will be considerable. For example, in Newfoundland, according to the Canadian Labour Congress study-I know the government does not agree with it but even it agrees that there will be a loss of money in the form of benefits to Newfoundland-it estimates that the loss to Newfoundland would be $51 million in benefits; the loss to Prince Edward Island, $32 million; the loss to Nova Scotia, $29 million; the loss to New Brunswick, $148 million; and the loss to Quebec, $224 million.
The government will say that it intends to put back some of those moneys in the form of training and development but there is no assurance in the bill that those moneys will go back to the province that is losing them in the form of benefits. If there are people unemployed, for example, in Nova Scotia and their benefits are cut and the total loss to Nova Scotia in the form of benefits as a result of a more difficult qualification period and a shorter benefit period is $29 million, the province is concerned that that money is not going to be going to Nova Scotia with all that unemployment. It wants some assurance that the money is going to come back and that is why the provincial ministers wanted to appear. By the way, they have already applied to appear before the Senate committee. They want time to prepare themselves and so on.
There is good reason for the government to extend the variable entrance requirement for several months but not necessarily for the whole year. There is good reason to accept the fact that many groups that have not been heard should be heard on this bill, if they believe in democracy on that side of the House. There is good reason for the regions to be concerned that they will be short-changed as a result of Bill C-21.
I emphasize that what we are asking for today is not to be considered a vote of confidence. What we are asking
Supply
for is a motion or a bill to extend the variable entrance requirement and we in this party make the commitment that we would not debate the measure at all. We would pass it immediately if the minister brought it in as has been done in previous years in the month of December.
As we approach the Christmas season, I appeal to the government to be sensible on this, to show some kindness and understanding and to accept the fact that both Houses of this Parliament need to debate and consider measures. We hope that it will bring in, as it has done in previous years, the variable entrance requirement measure to extend it for three or four months or whatever is reasonable in the circumstances. I hope before the day is over and after listening to the minister, she will agree to that.
I know she may say as the House leader said, "Well, let the Senate pass it in a few weeks". I hope that she would reconsider that because if the Senators do that, they are going to turn down many serious groups that want to be heard on the bill. As I say, let us just give them a few weeks to discuss this and have hearings on a bill of such importance.
Members opposite agree that this bill is of great importance. They think it is one of the major planks in their reform as they see it. If that is the case, if they have great confidence in their measure, then I suggest they should give ample time, not unreasonable time and not time to block the measure, but reasonable time to deal with this.
I plead with the minister to bring in a measure to extend the variable entrance requirement. It will not be a question of confidence in the government and we will pass it without any debate whatsoever.

speechtext:
As the member for Kamloops mentioned earlier this morning, he wrote a letter to the government House leader. With the permission of the House, I would like to read bits of it. There is no use reading it all:
For years all parties have cooperated to give swift passage to an annual bill which provides entrance requirements for UI, and enabled Canadians living in regions of high unemployment to receive benefits with a shorter eligibility period. C-21 was expected to obviate the need for such a bill this year.
He concludes by saying:
I suggest it would be most prudent for the House to pass in the customary one-sitting fashion a bill to extend varying entrance requirements until such time as C-21 is proclaimed.

Supply
I would like to commend the Official Opposition for having brought this matter before the House today on its opposition day. I think it is worth repeating parts of that motion as well:
That this House declare its willingness to pass such a measure in no more than one sitting; and
That, for greater certainty, this House declare that the passage of this motion does not constitute a vote of non-confidence in the government.
From the point of view of the opposition, I cannot think of anything which would be more indicative of the desire of the Opposition to co-operate with the government in alleviating what is going to be a very severe situation for some people who become unemployed if the action which has taken place in previous years is not also taken this year.
I have no idea what the Senate will do with Bill C-21.1 do not know if what the Senate does with Bill C-21 is the pertinent issue facing us today or over the next few weeks. The pertinent issue is that there are going to be people who need unemployment assistance, and unless we make the usual yearly accommodation for the varying rates, people are going to suffer. That is the issue.
The fact of the matter is, of course, that Bill C-21 is also an issue in this and I suspect that what really is occurring is that the government is using the fact that the bill is in the Senate and may or may not be held up as a weapon to force the Senate to come back quickly with the legislation so it can be in place by January 6. I think that is shameful, shameful but I guess understandable.
This is not all that much of a departure from the actions of the government over the last six or seven months since Bill C-21 was first introduced. Bill C-21 itself is a very severe measure and I think it can be interpreted in almost all respects as being a measure to punish those who become unemployed. There is no other way to see it, in spite of the fact that the government claims it is a new measure which will take Canada into the 21st Century.
In a previous speech I made in the House, I referred to it as being into the 20th century. I think that is far more applicable. We are not going from the 19th to the 20th Century, but probably more likely from the 20th back to
the 19th. We certainly are not going into the 21st century with this legislation.
At every stage of the passage of Bill C-21 through the House, the government introduced closure. I do not know in this context if it is acceptable to use the word "he" or not, but it gives the lie, I think, to the government's assurance that it had unanimous approval of the House when the bill went to the Senate. If I cannot use that word, at least it certainly casts into a great deal of doubt whether or not the bill going to the Senate had the unanimous approval of this House. It certainly was not overwhelming at all, it was overwhelming opposition, not only by the members of the opposition, but by the Canadian public expressing itself before the committee as the committee did its work across the country.
The fact that the government is doing what it is doing in relation to the non-extension of variable entrance requirements and the fact that I think it used closure-I think closure is also one of the things which ties in so closely with what the government is doing-is a very good example that indeed this is not a progressive measure at all, at least in so far as those who have become unemployed are concerned. It may be in so far as some yet to be explained, yet to become obvious agenda of the government. It may be beneficial in some sense but not in so far as the unemployed are concerned or even as the training which the government so frequently expressed as being one of the underlying reasons for it to do what it is doing is concerned.
What is really happening as far as Bill C-21 is concerned, as far as the non-approval of the varying entrance requirements is concerned, is that the government is indicating in no uncertain terms to the House and to the Canadian public where it stands.
Where the government stands is not at all on the side of the oppressed, but it is in fact becoming one of the major oppressors in the social fabric of Canada by using people who are in such an unfortunate situation as pawns in what is only a perceived argument between itself and the Senate.
Oppressed may possibly be a strong word, but let us look at the group of people who will be primarily affected by Bill C-21 and as well by the non-passage of the variable entrance requirements for people who become unemployed.

I have a list here of some of the jobs that are available. We keep hearing reference made to all these jobs that are available. If time permits, I will probably be making reference to those a little bit later, but for the time being, I would like to refer to some of the hourly rates that are available for some of the jobs that one would find if you went to the local unemployment insurance office: A delivery driver, $5 an hour; a landscape worker; $7 an hour; a seamstress, rather a highly skilled person, I would suggest, a mere $5.50 an hour; and floorwalkers, $5.25 an hour.

speechtext:
If we go into another region of Canada, we find that waiter/waitresses are making the princely sum of $4.50 an hour.
I think that was an uncalled for reference. Streetwalker, no, I think not. I doubt if too many members of the opposition have much of an idea of what a streetwalker would be making.
A fish plant worker-the list goes on and on and the rates go on and on. I would like to point out that those are an extremely disadvantaged group of people when we are talking about unemployment insurance which is precisely what we are talking about. These are people who are making those rates, the highest of which I see on my list is $8 an hour which in a year is somewhere around $16,500. For even a single person, that is below the poverty level in most regions of the country.
Even at that, if you become unemployed, that is not the rate you receive. If you were making $5 an hour when you were working and you become unemployed, the rate you now receive is $3 an hour because you receive only 60 per cent. Part of the rationale of the government bringing in Bill C-21 in the first place was because the system was being so severely abused. Can you imagine anyone quitting work intentionally, making $5 an hour so that they can subsequently earn $3? I think it shows how abusive, crass and uncaring, and, yes, how oppressing, Bill C-21 is.
Speaking of quitting, on that same job of $5 an hour, going to $3 an hour under ordinary circumstances, after a waiting period, of course, which will be increased by Bill C-21, if you quit voluntarily without just cause which, with all due respect to some changes in Bill C-21, is still going to be difficult enough to substantiate even in the
Supply
most extreme cases of unsafe work places, racial and sexual discrimination and so on, the rate you would be receiving on unemployment insurance would be $2.50 an hour. It varies accordingly if you happen to be fortunate enough to make $6 an hour. At the 60 per cent rate, you would be earning $3.60, but if you quit for any of the justifiable reasons, then, of course, you do not receive a penalty after you have established that it was justifiable, you would receive the $3.60. But if you could not substantiate it, you would receive a mere $3 an hour. That is not a lot of money, and certainly not something that anyone is going to get wealthy on.
These are the people whom the government is holding to ransom with respect to the non-voluntary passage today, if you will. Certainly the New Democratic Party is willing, as is the Official Opposition having already stated so, to pass that legislation with no interference whatsoever. I suspect that if we were to do it in the usual manner, you may possibly miss it if you blinked. It could be accomplished that quickly.
Another disturbing aspect of what I have just finished describing is that most of these people are women. Many of them are single-parent mothers who, in addition to not making very much money and having a tremendously difficult time supporting their families on low rates of pay, are also working part-time jobs.
I know the government has reiterated many times that it has created more than a million jobs, but the fact of the matter is that statistics show that most of these people are still working part time. The way statistics operate, the way Statistics Canada does its reporting, one has to work the required number of hours a month to be able to qualify as a full-time worker.
Many of these people are working at two and perhaps three jobs and, believe it or not, the hours are cumulative in so far as the reporting of the numbers are concerned. Persons working at perhaps as many as three jobs would be classified as being full-time workers if they put in the required number which I believe is 28 hours per week. These are the people who are being held to ransom as a result of the non-voluntary, quick passage of the legislation which has gone through so expediently in previous years.

We have not really talked about another group of Canadian citizens who are going to be tremendously adversely affected should this not receive quick passage. I refer to the single- parent mothers and of course that implies there are children involved. I refer not only to single-parent mothers. Of course there are men who work at these low-paying jobs as well. Not being able to qualify for unemployment insurance in a reasonable length of time in an area with very high unemployment will severely affect even more children than it will people unemployed.
The number of people who will be unemployed is a rather interesting subject to talk about. Earlier on in history, not early in the history of Bill C-21 but about midway through, after the opposition parties had been trying for a long period of time to get the impact figures on the changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act, government numbers showed that somewhere around
30.000	would be totally excluded. Subsequent studies have shown that the numbers are much greater than that, ranging as high as 150,000. Probably a figure of
130.000	would be very close to the number of people excluded all together from receiving unemployment insurance, bearing in mind that the people we are talking about are very low-paid workers, part-time workers, mostly women.
Again I remind the House and Canadians that that is only the number of individuals who will not be receiving unemployment benefits. It does not-and I want to emphasize this-take into account the numbers of children who will be so adversely affected by these changes in Bill C-21 and by the non-passage of the variable entrance requirements rates.
I would remind the House that a week or a week and a half ago we had a New Democratic Party opposition day with reference to the plight of children, the tremendously dire conditions in which so many of these absolutely defenceless Canadian citizens find themselves through absolutely no fault of their own. I would suggest that their unemployed parents find themselves in that position for the most part, for the overwhelming part, through no fault of their own as well.
I would certainly commend the previous leader of our party for having spoken so eloquently on the subject of starvation among children in Canada and their plight. I
think that is something we must remember when we talk about the issues before the House today.
I guess it becomes part of the social balance sheet. When the committee travelled across the country we heard representations from a large group of people. There is no question about that. When we were in northern Ontario reference began to be made by cities and municipalities which were speaking not only for themselves but for the provinces in which they were located. The city of Vancouver felt so strongly about the changes which were going to be occurring and the adverse effect which was going to be felt by it that the mayor of the city of Vancouver made the presentation on behalf of the city.
The imbalance in the social balance sheet is going to come about as a result of not implementing the variable rates for however long a period. I would not even want to put a time limit on it, for however long it requires for the democratic process to wend its way through the system it is going to be tremendously severe as are the changes to Bill C-21. We have these two things going along in an almost parallel fashion.
The government is going to have to one day wake up to the fact that it has made a tremendous mistake in judging the temperament of the Canadian people, in thinking that Canadian people would accept these changes to such a valuable social program.
I reiterate that the New Democratic Party is willing, as the member for Kamloops indicated, to pass this as speedily as possible so that the dire effects of not passing it do not necessarily have to come to pass. Certainly, if it does not happen, the government will have this down upon its head and will have to suffer the consequences.

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, without question this is a very important motion that we are debating today, and I do welcome this opportunity. I thank the member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace for raising this issue because it is an important one.
I remind the House that it passed Bill C-21, an act to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, last November 7. In so doing the House assured the full protection of all workers across Canada who found themselves in economically distressed regions or circumstances.
December 5, 1989

While I welcome the debate the motion is an unfortunate one. Year after year governments have extended the variable entry requirement each time for only one more year. In contrast, this government has presented Bill C-21 as a genuine response to regional variations. Bill C-21 not only provides for the variable entrance requirements but it does so on a permanent basis. In effect it provides all Canadians with fair access to income support in times of unemployment.
Yet, while this government has demonstrated leadership by introducing the Labour Force Development Strategy, our friends across the way are spinning then-wheels in the mind set of a decade ago.

During the past five years, this government has taken measures that previous administrations had scrupulously avoided. The challenges of the 1990s demand genuine leadership, real solutions and at times, the ability to make difficult choices.
The government has shown that leadership, not only by making changes in the unemployment insurance program but also by setting up agreements for regional economic development, obtaining the free trade agreement and providing for prosperity and growth, a fact that did not escape the OECD. And on top of that, we have created jobs, real jobs, more than one million since 1984.

We have replaced the former make-work programs of the former government with concrete long-term strategies for job creation that spell greater opportunities for the development of our human resources and for individual achievement. Bill C-21 is part and parcel of this government's Labour Force Development Strategy which provides for an additional $775 million in new programming to meet the needs of the unemployed and to upgrade the skills of the labour force.
Bill C-21 calls for change, yes, but it does so in a balanced and fair manner, and it does so in particular by providing for a flexible variable entrance requirement.
Let me remind the House of the other ways that Bill C-21 will help Canadians. With the goal of developing our human resources, Bill C-21 significantly increases funding for training under section 26 and the new subsection 26(1) of the UI Act. In total $1 billion will be
Supply
available from the UI account for income support and courses for UI recipients.
Bill C-21 allows UI recipients with viable business plans to capitalize their benefits to help defray business start-up costs. The spin-offs from such support go far beyond simply getting claimants off UI and on to their feet. Whole communities will benefit economically. In the experience of other countries which have this kind of provision, such entrepreneurship has created an additional job for each new business start-up.
As well, the bill allows UI recipients to receive their UI payments in a lump sum, another flexible way in which recipients can benefit. That will allow some of them who wish to move to areas with better job prospects to do so. The changes also provide older workers with expanded retraining and job-finding services.
The government was determined to bring the UI Act into line with the realities of today's work patterns which have changed and with the equity provisions of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. I remind hon. members that Bill C-21 provides for 15 weeks of maternity benefits during the period surrounding the birth of a child, but it also makes available 10 weeks of parental benefits for natural and adoptive parents, for either mother or father or shared between them.
Furthermore, Bill C-21 ensures that claimants have the flexibility to draw a combination of special benefits up to a maximum of 30 weeks. I would remind hon. members that until we introduced these changes or until these changes are passed it was not possible to be pregnant and also sick. We have made that much better for women who have need of special benefits. Indeed we are getting many phone calls now from women who are looking forward to the new benefits that they will receive, hopefully in January.
Finally this bill extends UI eligibility to those who work after they reach age 65, something else that will bring our unemployment insurance in line with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms and will also benefit those who are leading active and vigorous lives in the workforce beyond age 65.
All these changes made Canada's unemployment insurance program more equitable, more flexible, and more relevant to evolving social and work patterns. At the same time it sets out to reduce disincentives to work,

December 5, 1989
Supply
particularly in areas with strong economies and with low unemployment.
We have reached a time in Canada where we cannot afford to sacrifice a large part of the population, individual Canadians, to unemployment or to underemployment when that is not what those Canadians are seeking.
Canada is in the midst of one of the most exciting and challenging economic transitions in our history; the transition from a traditional resource-based economy to one where knowledge and skills and human resources play an increasingly central role. This transition not only confronts Canada but the entire industrialized world, and Canada has to be ready. Our competitive standing in that world will depend on how well we prepare ourselves over the next few years. It is especially important that we continue to adapt our labour market programs to the reality of a changing economy.
Canadians face a future where change is the only constant and where constant adaptation to new technologies, new market conditions and new skill requirements is imperative for the workers themselves to lead satisfying lives and for small businesses and for large companies, but most particularly of course for individual Canadians.
Bill C-21 is part of Canada's adaptation to change, as is the rest of the Labour Force Development Strategy which we announced in April. It works to develop and manage our human resources more effectively with the help of our private sector partners. All told for unemployed Canadians the strategy represents more support of activities like training and skill development that lead directly to jobs.
For Canadians who have jobs the strategy represents a chance to maintain and upgrade skills in response to changing demands. It encourages government's partners-labour, business and educators; we are not in this alone-to work together and build a workforce that is equipped for the future.
Because the co-operation of our partners is so important we tailored Bill C-21 as closely as possible to the labour market needs of Canadians. The contents of this bill, contrary to what hon. members opposite have insinuated, have been scrutinized from every conceivable angle. I would remind members that there were over 200
presentations to the committee when that legislative committee travelled across the country.
In designing the bill we considered as well the Macdonald Commission, the Forget inquiry, the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration, and the de Grandpre advisory council. We listened to Canadians and parliamentarians and we did make several amendments, I would remind members, in consideration of their suggestions.
Currently I am consulting with business, labour, nongovernmental organizations and community groups to design new training programs. I must say that that is a real breakthrough in terms of the co-operation and the partnerships that can be built to deal with the realities of the workplace. I would certainly say that we have given Canadians a more than fair chance to tell us what they think about the bill.
The government, as always, had to make some difficult decisions when this bill was drafted. In a country so diverse, I think it is accurate to say that compromise is almost always a part of the solution to our problems. We believe strongly that this bill reflects the demands that Canadians presented to us.
With respect to the entrance requirements that we are debating today, it brings the UI system into line with new economic situations such as, for example, the booming area around metropolitan Toronto. Certainly Bill C-21 allows the UI system to differentiate more fairly between regions that need lots of support and those that need less support.
I think it is quite unfair that neither the Senate nor the opposition recognizes that the solution to the present variable entrance problem already exists in Bill C-21. Instead of taking that solution to its logical conclusion they choose to ignore it.
Let me remind the House that it was always our intention to use UI changes to help free up the necessary resources to expand developmental programming. We think this is a good use of the fund. I should point out, although I hate to say it, that this is not a new idea. It has been done before. The objective of these modest changes that we are making was to encourage a greater commitment to the labour market.
December 5, 1989

I would remind members that the former government did exactly the same thing. At the time when the member for Winnipeg South Centre was the Minister of Employment and Immigration he signed a report called Unemployment Insurance in the 1980s which said that when the 10 to 14-week variable entrance requirement was introduced in 1978, 87 per cent of people affected in the Atlantic provinces found the two extra weeks needed to qualify and 40 per cent of those affected elsewhere found the up to six weeks they needed. When the entrance requirements for new entrants and re-entrants were raised to 20 weeks in 1979, there was an immediate sharp rise in the number of claimants applying with exactly 20 insurable weeks, especially in the Atlantic provinces.
As an example, the number of claims established in New Brunswick with exactly 20 insurable weeks virtually doubled between 1978 and 1980. Those additional work weeks in both years were secured in spite of continuing unemployment in the range of 8.4 per cent, somewhat higher than we have today.
Now that is a report on what happened when the variable entrance requirements were changed before. It is signed, as I said, by the neighbour of the member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace, the member for Winnipeg South Centre.
By expanding the active program assistance we are going much further and doing much more for people, because UI recipients will be in a better position to secure long-term and productive work.
Let me also remind the House that workers in areas of high unemployment often must fight tenaciously to preserve their places in the workforce. If Bill C-21 continues to be delayed until it is too late to make the necessary changes for the new year, some workers in Canada will find themselves facing difficult times, and that is not why I entered public service. We are thinking about the needs of unemployed Canadians.
Clearly the opposition and the Senate have the ability to permit the changes that we have proposed in Bill C-21. If they choose not to let the bill through, the consequences are evident. The government has provided the solution to the existing variable entrance rate which we believe has been an inadequate response to Canadians who find themselves out of work. We have modernized the entrance requirements to suit the current economic situation of our communities.
Supply
In addition, we are altering the UI program to allow those Canadians most in need to get training and other types of help so that they can find lasting, secure and satisfying jobs.

Bill C-21 arises from the demands that our country must meet in order to respond to new challenges on a more competitive world market. Thanks to this bill, the government has been able to provide a fair program that will ensure income security is maintained during periods of unemploymnent. We worked very hard, we put our solution before the House of Commons, and the House approved that solution.

The hon. member for Saskatoon-Dundum was talking about what would happen to Canadians if we do not support the motion of the opposition today. However, what Canadians are waiting to see is whether its representatives follow the lead this government has provided to ensure that deserving Canadians receive what they are entitled to in the coming year.
Let me remind hon. members that this is not just the variable entrance requirements that are at risk if they do not proceed expeditiously in the other place. The benefits to expectant mothers, to fathers, to those over 65, and the expansion of the Community Futures Program which is there to help people in regions that have particular needs will not be expanded unless Bill C-21 goes through. The expansion of the program for social assistance recipients will not go through either, unless we have some sensitivity to all the reforms we have put into Bill C-21. I may remind hon. members of the withdrawal of the repeater provision for seasonal workers which will help many of the people in the regions of Canada through our new bill.
I have already pointed out that when this same approach was taken under the former government, whose members are sitting over there snickering at what we are trying to accomplish, the people did find work; they were better off.
I would hope that members would join me today in urging the other place to hasten the passage of Bill C-21 so Canadian workers will not only have their variable entrance requirements but can develop their skills for the 1990s and will be able to take advantage of all of the advantages that we have put into Bill C-21.

December 5, 1989

Madam Speaker, I have some questions for the hon. minister. There is no doubt that the minister believes that the provisions in Bill C-21 are good ones. They are her proposals; it is her bill. She believes in them strongly and thinks that they will be good for the Canadian people, but she must recognize that many Canadians do not agree that all the measures in that bill are good. As a matter of fact, when the House of Commons committee sat throughout the country, 157 out of 202 groups opposed many of the measures in the bill and opposed the bill.
The minister must recognize that there are people who in good faith do not accept her point of view with respect to that bill. The minister must recognize as well that many believe that the bill will impact on them in a negative way. As I pointed out, there were 2.2 million claimants under the unemployment insurance system last year, and many of them believe that they will be impacted upon in a negative way as a result of this bill.
The minister must also accept that a lot of individuals, groups and experts were not heard by the House of Commons committee. We did our best in the committee. We heard many trade unions, many chambers of commerce and many social groups but, as I pointed out, we made a decision that we could not hear provincial government representatives. We heard very few academics and we did not hear the Economic Council, the Canadian Council for Labour Productivity, and so on. The minister must recognize that there are many people who would like to have their say on this bill who have not been heard. There are many people who feel it impacts in a negative way and many people who do not agree with it.
My first question is: Does the Minister not accept that those people who are concerned about the bill should have a right to be heard?
My second question is: What is wrong with a temporary extension to the variable entrance requirement? We are not suggesting in this party that the answer to unemployment insurance problems is a 10 to 14-week variable entrance requirement. As a matter of fact, I was a member of the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration in the last Parliament which passed a unanimous report with a Conservative
majority. The chairman of the committee is the present Whip of the Conservative Party. We recommended that there be a flat 10 weeks, entrance requirement right across the country no matter what the rate of unemployment because we felt it was too difficult and unfair to have a variable entrance requirement. That was after a lot of study and many hearings before that committee.
All we are asking is that the government extend the variable entrance requirement for a reasonable period of time to allow those who want to be heard in the Senate to be heard. I am asking the minister: What is wrong with such a temporary extension?
I would not support that the Senate, the non-elected body, block this bill on a permanent basis, but I think they have a right and a duty to give reasonable attention to those who want to be heard.
Finally, the minister says there has been a lot of consultation on this bill. Does she not understand that consulting on a selective basis in her department or in her office with her officials is not the same as consulting publicly before a House of Commons or Senate committee where the proceedings are open to the public, the press and are reported? There is quite a difference between that kind of consultation in a public, open way and consultation in her office.
I ask her what is wrong with giving a right to be heard to those who ought to be heard and must be heard? What is wrong with a temporary extension of the variable entrance requirement? Can she not see the difference between public consultation and private consultation in her office or in her department?

Madam Speaker, I do not think this government has anything to learn from the opposition about the right of people to be heard. It is not a case of having consultations behind closed doors in my office. That is certainly not the way we have approached it. In fact, there is a series of public discussions and forums going on right across the country with labour and management even as we speak. They are being organized by the Canadian Labour and Management Productivity Centre in order to get a variety of opinions on the training programs and the skills development side. This is a real breakthrough. It is not something the opposition ever did when it was in government.

We have made a real point of ensuring that the voices of labour, business, and educators are heard and particularly groups such as the Canadian Congress for Learning Opportunities for Women. We will be consulting with a number of people within the native and disabled communities who will also make their voices heard as we develop the training part of the program.
Let me say as well that I have no objection to the people in the Senate calling their witnesses and hearing people they believe would be helpful to them. Since the other place is not sitting this week they have some considerable time in which to do that in committee. I understand they will hear before they are finished-and I respect not only their right to do this but the responsibility they have to do this-a variety of points of view. In fact there are some people, as I have been told by some of our members in the other place, who can come to explain just how the benefits will work.
It is also important to point out to the 2.2 million claimants last year, some of whom are concerned that they will be impacted on negative ways, that the average usage of unemployment insurance was really well below the maximum number of weeks that people are allowed to utilize. Under the new bill in Newfoundland, for example, the maximum duration of benefits under Bill C-21 is 50 weeks in all three regions. That is exactly what it was before. The variable entrance requirement in the new bill is exactly what it was before. What we are going to see is some improvement in places like Atlantic Canada in terms of the flexibility that we are putting into the program and how it is going to be so much better for people.
I am sure when people come to the other place that they can call the witnesses of their choice. If they choose to hear provincial governments, academics or whomever, I am sure they will do that.
I am very proud of this bill. I am looking forward to hearing the kind of debate and the kind of people who do come forward to the committee.
When you talk about the 157 groups who are opposed to the bill, I know that they are all opposed to it for different reasons. Some support one part while the next person who comes in is against it. I rise to call on the government and in particular on the minister to prevent hardship in the high unemployment areas of Canada.
On January 6, if the unemployment insurance bill, Bill C-21, has not received Royal Assent, then, as we all know, the uniform entrance requirements will come into force on a nation-wide basis. In certain areas of this country this will add to and create a hardship. I refer most particularly to those areas in Atlantic Canada, in Cape Breton, in Newfoundland and in New Brunswick. Indeed, many of the areas of the Atlantic, already hard pressed by this government, will suffer untold exacerbation of difficulty.
There are two points to be considered. One is the usual parliamentary process involving the other place. The second is the fair treatment of Canadian workers while Parliament does its work in its normal course.
The people in my riding of Halifax will not suffer greatly in the short term if Bill C-21 is delayed without the introduction of the usual variable entrance requirement bill. Indeed, they will be better off in the short [DOT] term than they will under Bill C-21.

It was so important that the timetable was moved up so that these variable entrance requirements could be brought in. Is it less important in 1989? Is it less important to the people of the economically depressed areas of this country that they have an opportunity to survive-and I use that word advisedly, too-the very hard winter that lies ahead of them?

The hon. minister calls this motion unfortunate. Bill C-21 is unfortunate. It is unfortunate for fisheries workers. It is unfortunate for rural seasonal workers. It is unfortunate for the urban poor, and it sure is unfortunate for Canadian women. In fact, this bill is an institutionalized misfortune for our country.
The hon. minister says that we in Canada are going through an exciting transition. That must be a huge comfort to the people of Summerside. I am sure that it engenders great joy in Lunenburg and Lockeport where the fish plants are closing. Indeed, this transition is so exciting that it is a wonder that Atlantic Canadians are not dancing in the streets.
The minister tells us constantly, and we have been hearing it ever since the introduction of this unfortunate bill, about the training programs in Bill C-21, particularly the training programs as they affect women. This is another fiction that is being perpetrated upon the people of Canada.
I spoke last week to the operator of a medium-sized business in my riding of Halifax. I asked him about the training programs for women. He said, "Yes, it is going to be great. I can train my receptionist to work on the word processor and I can train my secretary to become a bookkeeper". I said, "Are you not going to be going outside and training new people so you can hire them and add to the number of employed?" "Oh, no, I don't have to do that", he said, "I can train in house and save myself a whole lot of money". That saving will be on the backs of the taxpayers of Canada, without assisting in any way the unemployment rate, particularly for women. It is great stuff.
The bill itself will make it more difficult, as we already know and as we have already heard, to qualify for unemployment insurance by increasing the qualification periods. We know it will cut off claimants sooner by shortening the benefit period. It will increase the penalty for those who voluntarily quit. Of course the whole voluntarily quit provision is a fascinating one
I spent four years in a previous life chairing the Unemployment Insurance Appeal Board in my riding of Halifax. I heard about some of the voluntary quits, the voluntary quits that had to do with everything from sexual harassment to absolutely untenable working conditions. Sure, the unemployment Insurance Act needs

reform. It needs lots of reform. But the reform should go in favour of the workers of Canada and not against them.
It should not be a punch in the stomach or a belt in the jaw. It should be some form of support and some recognition by the government that the workers of Canada do suffer stoppages of employment from time to time. This is an insurance program
The injustice from the voluntary quits arises when someone quits a job for what he or she believes to be just cause, but just cause under this bill is something that will be increasingly difficult to prove.
I mentioned earlier that in my riding of Halifax if the VER does not go through, if the government does not bring in this bill as it has traditionally, and if Bill C-21 does not pass until after the other place has followed its duly appointed constitutional itinerary, then Halifax will not suffer all that badly. Halifax suffers from a disparity in incomes. Because of this disparity in incomes there is an almost false rate of unemployment. To be unemployed in Halifax is every bit as bad-sometimes worse-as it is to be unemployed in Cape Breton because you do not have the support systems and the family support that is traditional in Cape Breton Island and in the rural areas of Nova Scotia. All of the problems of urban alienation affect the poor and the unemployed in a city like Halifax.
The rate is skewed because of this disparity. We have an area that covers my city of Halifax, that of my learned colleague from Dartmouth and down the eastern shore of Nova Scotia where employment opportunities outside the fishery are rare. Of course we know what has happened to the fishery in Atlantic Canada. Consequently, there is a grinding poverty facing unemployed workers in the urban regions of Nova Scotia this winter. This government is not prepared to do anything to assist that while the Parliament of Canada goes through its normal process.
Why is the government not moving the VER bill this year? Is it an attempt to make the duly appointed members of the other place look like the villains? Is it an attempt to make it seem as though this bill was stalled there just to flex its muscles with a complete disregard for Canadians on UI? If this is the case, then a fraud is being perpetrated on the people of Canada because the

other place is doing its duly constitutionally asked for job.

I cannot imagine what is on the minds of our government masters by refusing to take this opportunity to ensure that Canadians are protected and that Canadians in Atlantic Canada, northern Ontario, parts of Quebec, in the north and so on will not have to look toward January and February with fear and trepidation because they fear for their very survival due to the actions of their government.

Madam Speaker, unless the regional entrance requirement is implemented, we will have regional tragedies, especially in the Atlantic region, among fishermen, steel workers, miners, and all the people working in fish processing plants. The winter will be very difficult for families in our region.
The federal government must not make the situation any worse. It is time to show compassion and understanding for regional disparities.

It is time for the government to show that it cares something for the hard-pressed people of Canada. It is time, after the disastrous actions of this government in its budget and in other actions taken in the spring and the summer, to say, "We understand what the people of the Atlantic in particular will go through this winter without the normal bill on the variable entrance requirement".
Here we have a cri de coeur which goes to the government and says, "For God's sake, do something for the people who deserve your protection".

Madam Speaker, I am sure the hon. member who just spoke, and spoke so well, understands that a solid unemployment insurance system is not only good for the workers who are unemployed but also extremely helpful to the communities in which they live when they are unemployed.
When an unemployed worker receives unemployment insurance he or she spends that money on groceries, on rent, on fuel for automobiles, on children's clothing and so on. The money is spent and it circulates in the community. During the great depression before 1940 when we did not have unemployment insurance and people were unemployed and did not have that money to spend, the recession, or the depression, the slow-down, snow-balled and galloped and the comer stores that used to sell to those people went bankrupt. The whole economy went further down the drain. That is prevented with a solid unemployment insurance system. Therefore the member probably knows and would admit that it is important not only for the individual unemployed but also for the community.
As a result of Bill C-21 unemployment insurance benefits will be reduced by $1.5 billion. The government is taking $1.5 billion away from regular benefits.
When you break that down, it means that her province, the province of Nova Scotia, will lose $29 million that would have gone into that province in unemployment insurance benefits. That money will not be going into the province. Perhaps the government might spend some of
December 5, 1989

that money on training in the province, but there is no assurance of that.
We were not able to hear in the House of Commons committee provincial government representatives. We were not able to hear people who looked at the impact on the provinces from a macroeconomic point of view.
Does the hon. member not agree that it is reasonable now for the Senate to hear these people, especially since they have the new maps of the new regions, who can inform Parliament as to what the impacts will be from an economic point of view of withdrawing these moneys from provinces like Nova Scotia or New Brunswick? Can she not make the point that it is not we Liberals, senators or members of Parliament, who want to be heard, that it is the people from these regions who want to be heard to make their points with respect to these economic arguments?

Madam Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague from Notre-Dame-de-Grace for his comments. Mr. Speaker, as the economic conditions in Cape Breton continue to worsen, this government is doing its utmost to try to cut out the underpinnings of the economy which still exists. One of those prime underpinnings is VIA Rail.
VIA Rail is vitally important to the economy of Cape Breton. This government has manipulated with Canadian National to do away with VIA. Now CN is doing its
best to try to get rid of the business it presently has in eastern Nova Scotia. Three-quarters of all the container traffic that once went between North Sydney and Port aux Basques, Newfoundland, is now going between Halifax and St. John's. Mr. Speaker, Mr. Paul Stokaluk, a resident of Thunder Bay-Nipigon, recently travelled to Toronto with his wife. She required an extremely delicate eye operation. After the operation, Mrs. Stokaluk's doctor instructed her not to fly home because this form of travel would do further damage to her already sensitive eye. Following the doctor's advice, the Stokaluks returned to Thunder Bay on a sleeper car on VIA Rail. She was required to lie on her side all through the trip so as not to do further damage to this very sensitive area.
These concerned constituents called my office questioning what they would have done had Mrs. Stokaluk's operation been scheduled after January 15, 1990. That is the day when passenger rail service will no longer be available to the people in northern Ontario.
It is wrong to eliminate passenger train service in northern Ontario. It is unacceptable that this government eliminate a line which services over 300,000 residents of these communities. How else will the physically handicapped like Mrs. Stokaluk travel? How will the economically handicapped, those who cannot afford to fly and those who do not want to fly, travel throughout the north? It is wrong that these people and the 300,000 residents of Marathon, Terrace Bay, Schrieber, Nipigon, Red Rock, Thunder Bay, Ignace, Dryden, Kenora be denied passenger rail service after having it for over 104 years.

Mr. Speaker, recent figures released by Canada Customs and Excise revealed that Canadians, as well as visitors to Canada, are increasingly choosing the Blue Water Bridge in my riding of Sarnia-Lambton as their point of departure and entry into Canada. Throughout and including the spring and summer of 1989 the total number of travellers reached 2.7 million, up 4.4 per cent from the previous year. By the end of October, the figures show that traffic on the Blue Water Bridge had jumped by more than 250,000 vehicles during the first 10 months of 1989. In all, almost 3.9 million cars and trucks crossed the international span, an increase of more than 260,000 as compared to 1988.
In a border community such as ours these traffic figures are particularly welcome from a tourism perspective. The tourism industry has been an integral part of the local economy and the community, including our local tourism operators, is striving to have more of these travellers stop and appreciate the many sites and attractions of Sarnia-Lambton.
I urge all members of the House, visitors to Canada, indeed all Canadians, to circle the Blue Water Bridge when travelling to and from Canada. I invite you all to come and see and appreciate our beautiful community of Sarnia-Lambton and what it has to offer.

December 5, 1989
efficiency, lit the lights on the parliamentary Christmas tree in front of the Centre Block.

Mr. Speaker, nearly 5 million Canadians have difficulty reading a sign or an instruction book. The Conference Board of Canada has recently reported that about one-third of Canadian companies have difficulty introducing new technology because some of their employees are functionally illiterate.
Last year our government introduced the National Literacy Strategy to help address these problems. The strategy focuses on remedial and preventive actions to help those with literacy problems and especially to promote literacy with children.
The year 1990 has been designated by the United Nations as International Literacy Year. This government is already doing its part to address the literacy challenge. While the cost of illiteracy to our country's economic future is enormous, the cost to the people involved is tragic.

Mr. Speaker, as a defender of Meech Lake, which I believe strengthens Canada, I was disappointed in the speech made by the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard) in Toronto before a large and happy crowd of Canadian francophones from across this country who were celebrating Ontario's Bill 8, a major achievement by the Peterson government affirming the rights of the official language minority in this province.
I was there, and I saw how shocked and insulted people were by the minister's attack against Pierre Elliot Trudeau and the way he misrepresented that vision of Canada which had in fact furthered their cause tremendously.

One of Canada's fundamental characteristics is the existence of official language minority groups, both in and outside Quebec. Trudeau was aware of this and supported those groups. You don't beat Canada, Mr. Speaker, by rewriting its history.

Mr. Speaker, I want to ask the President of the Treasury Board about the government's mishandling of the strike of 2,200 federal ships' crew workers and over 1,400 federal hospital workers.
For two years the government has been trying to find every possible legal loophole to avoid bargaining in good faith. First, it bungled declaring these workers essential to the safety and security of the Canadian public. Then it spent months trying to get the courts to block the legal right of these workers to strike. It went through conciliation without ever putting a serious offer on the table. Now it is so threatened by people exercising their legal rights, it has gone to the courts to stop picketing and wants to order these people back to work.
How does the minister justify risking the safety and security of Canadians with these ham-handed bullying tactics? Will he state here and now that the government will get back to the bargaining table with a good offer, a serious offer and get this thing settled properly?
